level-1.title: Saving and spending
summary: Spending means you use money now.
Saving means you keep money for later.
You can put saved money in a piggy bank.
If you save ₹10 every week, you will have ₹40 after four weeks.
Saving helps you buy something bigger later.

questions.prompt: You save ₹5 every day for a week (7 days). How much will you have?

image.alt: A piggy bank with a week of coins beside it

questions.hint: Multiply 5 by how many days are in a week.

questions.prompt: You save ₹10 every week. After how many weeks will you have enough for a ₹90 toy?

image.alt: A calendar with several weeks marked

questions.hint: Divide the toy's price by how much you save each week.

questions.prompt: A cricket ball costs ₹150. You have ₹50 and get ₹20 pocket money each week. In how many weeks can you afford it?

image.alt: A cricket ball beside a savings jar

questions.hint: First find out how much more you need, then divide by your weekly pocket money.

level-2.title: Choosing to save or to spend
summary: Every rupee you spend is a rupee you cannot save.
A savings goal is a thing you are saving for, with a price and a date.
Write the goal down. A bicycle costs ₹4000. You save ₹200 each month.
₹4000 divided by ₹200 is 20. So the goal takes 20 months.
Small spends add up. ₹20 a day is ₹600 in one month.

questions.prompt: A bicycle costs ₹4000. You already have ₹800 saved, and you save ₹200 more each month. How many more months until you can buy it?

image.alt: A bicycle with a price tag and some coins already saved

questions.hint: First subtract what you already have, then divide by the monthly saving.

questions.prompt: You spend ₹20 a day on snacks and ₹15 a day on games, every day for 30 days. How much MORE do you spend on snacks than on games that month?

image.alt: A snack and a game token side by side

questions.hint: Find the daily difference first, then multiply by 30 days.

questions.prompt: You want to save ₹4000 for a bicycle by June, but you also plan to buy a ₹500 game every month until then. What happens to your savings goal?

image.alt: A savings target with a game purchase cutting into it

options.label: It will take much longer, or fail, because the game spending eats into the same money

questions.hint: Every rupee spent on the game is a rupee that cannot go toward the bicycle.

level-3.title: Saving, spending and opportunity cost
summary: Opportunity cost is what you give up when you choose.
If you spend ₹500 on headphones, the opportunity cost is the game you did not buy.
Pay yourself first means you save before you spend.
A common plan is to save 20 rupees out of every 100 you receive.
An emergency fund is money kept only for surprise problems.

questions.prompt: You earn ₹1000 and follow pay-yourself-first at a 20% rate, saving first and then spending ₹500 on headphones from what is left. What is the true opportunity cost of the headphones?

image.alt: Headphones next to a game box, with a savings jar already filled

options.label: The other thing worth ₹500 you could have bought with your spending money

questions.hint: Opportunity cost only concerns the money you chose to spend, not the money you saved first.

questions.prompt: You earn ₹1000 and follow pay-yourself-first at a 20% savings rate. How much do you save BEFORE spending anything?

image.alt: Money going into a savings jar before any spending happens

questions.hint: 20 percent of 1000 is saved first, before any spending happens.

questions.prompt: Your phone screen cracks and repair costs ₹800. You also want a new game worth ₹800. Which one should the emergency fund pay for, and why?

image.alt: A shield protecting a stack of coins, beside a cracked phone and a game

options.label: The phone repair — it is an unplanned problem, not a want you chose
The game — because you want it more
Both, since they cost the same

questions.hint: An emergency fund is for problems you did not choose, not things you wish for.
